title: VMware releases vSphere Express for virtualization on up to 128 cores
gist: Broadcom's VMware launched vSphere Express, a low-end per-core virtualization subscription (listed by TD Synnex at $9,600/year for up to 128 cores), an about-face after pushing SMBs toward the expensive VMware Cloud Foundation bundle. Analysts read it as a defensive move against customer churn to rivals, though many SMBs say Broadcom has lost their trust.

insights.claim: Broadcom's VMware announced vSphere Express, a per-core subscription for 'cost-effective essential virtualization' priced, per a spokesperson, significantly below the VVF and VCF bundles.
insights.speaker: Scharon Harding
insights.so_what: Marks a shift in Broadcom's VMware monetization strategy from forced bundling toward segment pricing.

insights.claim: IT distributor TD Synnex lists vSphere Express at $9,600 a year for up to 128 cores, with no lower price for fewer cores, which still challenges the smallest deployments.
insights.speaker: Scharon Harding
insights.so_what: A flat price floor limits how much SMB churn the product can actually stem.

insights.claim: vSphere Express includes vMotion live migration and high availability but supports only discrete instances without central management, and will be updated as often as VCF and VVF, unlike the long-stagnant vSphere Standard.
insights.speaker: Scharon Harding
insights.so_what: Feature limits are designed to keep larger customers on the higher-priced bundles.

insights.claim: VCF chief product officer Paul Turner said in September that Broadcom's sales incentives pushed its team to sell VCF and that VMware had 'too big a focus on VCF.'
insights.speaker: Paul Turner
insights.so_what: An internal admission that the bundling push overreached, suggesting further go-to-market adjustments.
insights.quote: too big a focus on VCF

insights.claim: vSphere Express suggests Broadcom, despite VMware's financial success under its ownership, may be worried about losing smaller customers and that its changes are pushing customers of all sizes to explore alternatives.
insights.speaker: Scharon Harding
insights.so_what: Signals that VMware's price-driven revenue gains may face growing churn risk.
insights.locator: While VMware has been financially successful

insights.claim: C4C Group chief technologist Nick Watson argued Express exists because customers priced VCF and began leaving, calling it Broadcom 'putting a door back on the building.'
insights.speaker: Nick Watson
insights.so_what: Independent read that customer defection, not goodwill, drove the product, implying real attrition.
insights.quote: My reading is that Express exists because customers looked at VCF, did the sums, and started packing. This is Broadcom putting a door back on the building.

insights.claim: Because migrating off VMware is costly and time-consuming, resource-constrained SMBs may find vSphere Express easier than switching platforms, though thousands that already migrated or lost their resellers will be hard to win back.
insights.speaker: Scharon Harding
insights.so_what: High switching costs protect VMware's base, but channel cuts have already given rivals a permanent foothold.
insights.locator: Migrating off VMware can be very costly

insights.claim: Since the Broadcom takeover VMware has cut channel partners, bundled products into a few expensive SKUs, and canceled plans to take its biggest clients direct.
insights.speaker: Scharon Harding
insights.so_what: Context for Broadcom's enterprise-focused playbook that drove margins but hurt the SMB channel.

insights.claim: Members IT Group CTO Dean Colpitts, a former VMware partner, said that even if adopting the new tier is easy, Broadcom has already shown customers and partners they can't be trusted.
insights.speaker: Dean Colpitts
insights.so_what: Partner distrust limits VMware's ability to recapture SMB share via the channel.
insights.quote: already shown both customers and partners they can't be trusted.
insights.locator: Speaking with Ars Technica in September
